title: Indian-Origin Student Vaibhav Bhaskar Sets Florida's Highest-Ever GPA at 11.99
excerpt: The Steinbrenner High School valedictorian took 44 advanced courses, earned an associate degree, and is headed to Duke University — all while running a nonprofit for the homeless.
body:
• Vaibhav Bhaskar graduated from Steinbrenner High School in Lutz, Florida, with an 11.99 weighted GPA — the highest ever recorded in the state.
  • He took 20 AP courses and 24 dual enrollment college classes, earning an associate degree alongside his high school diploma.
  • His achievement prompted Hillsborough County to overhaul its GPA weighting policy, which his principal called an academic "arms race."
  • Bhaskar will attend Duke University this fall to study finance and economics.

Vaibhav Bhaskar, an Indian-origin student from Lutz, Florida, has set a new state record with an 11.99 weighted grade-point average at Steinbrenner High School — surpassing the previous mark of 11.84 held by Gaither High School's Dylan Mazard since 2022. Bhaskar crossed the stage on May 24 at the Florida State Fairgrounds Expo Hall as valedictorian of the Class of 2026, ahead of 606 other graduates.

On a standard 5.0 scale, his GPA translates to a 4.93. But it was the eye-popping number on Hillsborough County's uncapped weighted scale that made national headlines — and forced the district to rethink how it calculates grades.

The Whiteboard Method

Behind the record was a deceptively simple habit. As a sophomore, Bhaskar hung a whiteboard in his bedroom and wrote down five goals for his high school career. The top two: "become valedictorian" and "break the state GPA record."

"Once I had those goals defined, and I had the mindset that I was going to accomplish those goals no matter what, from then on it just became about patience," he told the New York Post.

""It could've been a record in another state, maybe."</p>"

Patience, in Bhaskar's case, meant an extraordinary course load: 20 Advanced Placement courses and 24 dual enrollment college classes at the University of Florida, totalling 44 weighted courses across four years. He exhausted his school's AP offerings — every subject except AP Spanish II — and gave up his lunch period during junior year to squeeze in additional college-level coursework. By graduation, he had earned an associate degree alongside his diploma.

"I'm not all about school, school, school," he told the Tampa Bay Beacons. "I really enjoyed the AP classes. I loved learning about different things." His favourite was AP Macro/Micro Economics, which cemented his interest in finance.

An Indian-American Family's Quiet Support

Bhaskar's father, Bhaskar Malayappan, holds a Ph.D. in chemistry and did postdoctoral research in cancer biology — but said he had no idea his son was gunning for a state record. Malayappan, who had a 3.5 GPA in high school himself, only learned about the milestone after the numbers were frozen.

"We thought around his freshman year he was at 9," Malayappan told the Tampa Bay Beacons, "but the 11.99 was a surprise for us actually — shocked that it was the record."

The family's story is a familiar one in the Indian diaspora: parents with advanced degrees in the sciences, children charting their own course in the United States. But Bhaskar's path diverges from the stereotypical pre-med or engineering track. He is firmly pointed toward finance and economics, having interned at a stock transfer agency and a real estate private-equity firm, and published two research papers — one on financial risk analysis, the other on environmental conservation.

Beyond the GPA

Indian-American students have consistently excelled in American academic competitions, from spelling bees to science olympiads. Bhaskar's record adds another data point to that pattern, but what sets his story apart is the breadth of his engagement. At Steinbrenner, he served as chief financial officer of Back on Track America, a student-led nonprofit that organised donation drives for homeless shelters and food banks, logging over 300 volunteer hours. He also served as Vice President of Florida for Connect Me, a nonprofit offering free online tutoring to K-8 students.

His principal, Tiffany Ewell, was struck less by the number than by the maturity. "What impressed me most about Vaibhav is that even though he worked hard to achieve this goal, he seemed to put the achievement into perspective with the other aspects of his school experience," she told the Tampa Bay Beacons.

A Policy Overhaul — and What Comes Next

Bhaskar's record-setting GPA exposed a structural quirk in Hillsborough County's grading system: there was no cap on how many weighted points a student could accumulate. Ewell compared the resulting incentive structure to an "arms race." The district has since revised its policy for ninth graders starting in the 2023-2024 academic year, and many Florida districts are moving to an Honors Point Average system that averages grades rather than stacking them.

Bhaskar supports the change. "I actually absolutely agree with the change because it's a way more standardized way to calculate GPAs," he said. "My 11.99 GPA on our district's scale probably translates to a 4.93 on a standard 5.0 scale."

This fall, he heads to Duke University. He may not mention the record to his randomly assigned roommate. "I don't know if I'll tell him about the GPA — I might just keep it to myself," he said with a laugh. "It could've been a record in another state, maybe."
